      5. Carathéodory Measurability and the coincidence criterion for measures#

      An outer measure is defined on every subset of a set , however, according to Vitali’s counterexample, the identity may fail even though . Measures, on the other hand, are defined on -algebras, which are mostly proper subsets of , are functionals for which the identity above (and its countable analogue) holds by definition. We will show how to find a ``maximal’’ -algebra associated to such that is disjointly additive and therefore a measure. We will also show that for the Lebesgue outer measure, the resulting -algebra contains all Borel sets.

      Finally, we will prove a uniqueness principle: two measures that coincide on a suitable generating family coincide on the generated -algebra. This will allow us to prove that on the Borel -algebra, the Lebesgue meausure is indeed the unique one that assigns to intervals (or axes-parallel rectangles) their Euclidean volumes.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • Apply the Carathéodory criterion to contstruct -algebras.

      • Construct a complete measure by restricting an outer measure to its Carathéodory measurable sets.

      • Show that the Lebesgue measure is a measure on Borel sets.

      • Use Dynkin’s - theorem to prove that finite or -finite measures coincide on a generated -algebra under mild conditions.

      5.2.1 Open rectangles and Borel sets#

      The open rectangles used to define are already Carathéodory measurable. The point is that the part of a covering rectangle outside a fixed open rectangle can be covered by finitely many open rectangles, with an arbitrarily small increase in total volume.

      5.3 The coincidence criterion for measures#
